newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Burundi rebels slam easing of sanctions.
newsitem.headline: Burundi rebels slam easing of sanctions.

text.p: Burundi's main Hutu rebel group on Thursday condemned a "shocking" decision by regional leaders to ease sanctions on the ethnically-torn nation, saying it would jeopardise peace efforts.

Leonard Nyangoma's National Council for the Defence of Democracy (CNDD) said African leaders from Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Uganda, Zambia and Tanzania had also erred in inviting Tutsi military strongman Major Pierre Buyoya to Wednesday's summit in northern Tanzania.
"The CNDD must express its indignation. It is very shocking the conferring of head of state status on coup leader Buyoya," CNDD vice-president Christian Sendegeya told Reuters.

Sendegeya said the lifting of sanctions imposed last July to force Buyoya to return Burundi to constitutional rule and negotiate with the Hutu rebels would only benefit the country's ruling Tutsi military junta and its followers.
"The rural population does not benefit from this. The army continues to destroy peasants' homes. Peasants continue to live in swamp land to escape army killings," Sendegeya added.
In easing the embargo on Wednesday, African regional leaders urged Buyoya to disband "regroupment" camps for hundreds of thousands of civilians.
At a summit in Arusha with Buyoya, the leaders expanded the list of items excluded from sanctions imposed on Burundi since July 31 last year.

"The regional summit decided...to expand with immediate effect the easing of sanctions to include all food and food products, all items relating to education, construction materials as well as all types of medicines, agricultural items and inputs in order to alleviate the suffering of the people of Burundi," a statement said.
Fuel and food for aid agencies were already exempted from sanctions imposed six days after Buyoya seized power in a coup by the Tutsi-dominated army and ousted the Hutu president.

The president, Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, is still at the U.S. ambassador's residence in the capital Bujumbura. It was not clear if his fate was discussed at the Arusha meeting, the first attended by Buyoya since the coup.
The statement said the leaders called on the government to disband all "regroupment camps" and urged the creation of "a conducive spirit for national reconciliation and negotiations".
More than 200,000 Hutu and Tutsi civilians have been put in guarded camps since last year. The army says they protect people from rebels but aid agencies complain of their poor conditions.
Sendegeya said by lifting the sanctions, leaders were endangering the chances of a peaceful settlement in the war between Hutu rebels and Buyoya's army.
Buyoya has said he is ready for unconditional talks, which are opposed by hardline members of the Tuts -dominated army and former military ruler Jean-Baptiste Bagaza.

Wednesday's summit urged Buyoya to drop restrictions on the national assembly speaker and called for international pressure on Burundi through an arms embargo and the denial of visas to those obstructing the peace process.
In his latest report, U.N. Special Rapporteur for Human Rights Paulo Pinheiro said in February "there is no sign of the beginnings of a Burundi strategy for peace and reconciliation".
More than 150,000 people have died in massacres and fighting between the army and rebels since soldiers killed Burundi's first elected Hutu president in 1993.
